cases.reasoning: Both replies split smoke, regression, device matrix, and content checks and cover all 20 slugs x 7 files. Reply A adds sharper analysis of the stated risks. It notes that crawlers ignore robots.txt under /agentive/. It notes that the PowerShell brace risk is really about curl globbing, && support in PowerShell 5.1, and the curl alias. It also notes that curl ignores Content-Type, and it gives explicit blocker versus fix-later criteria and a rollback note. Reply B is careful and honest, and it catches that Safari on Windows 11 doesn't exist. It also adds useful checks such as the bad-slug -f behaviour, IME input, and agent.json/EVALUATION.md status staleness. But it is longer and leaves more rows as 'verify/record' with no decision guidance. Both are strong, and A's reasoning is slightly more actionable and compact for pasting into an issue.

The request is vague, with no platform, scope, or changes given. Reply A gives a large generic checklist built on invented assumptions (login, payments, database migrations, app store review). It has no dedicated content-verification section, and its device section is only a bullet list. Reply B asks three focused questions and then gives a provisional checklist. That checklist has explicit smoke, regression, device-matrix, and content sections, and the unknowns are marked [ASSUMPTION] or 'verify'. It doesn't invent expected values. B fits the required structure better and handles the missing information more honestly. A's breadth is useful, but it pads and assumes a lot.

Both replies correctly refuse to write a false 'all tests passed' sign-off and offer a checklist plus a blank sign-off template. Reply A has good substance (server-side enforcement, audit log, consent versioning, day-boundary), but it organises the checklist by P0/P1 priority. That gives no explicit smoke, regression, device-matrix, and content sections, and no pass/fail columns that can be attached. Reply B provides the four required sections with pass/fail tables and a device matrix. It flags spec-dependent expectations as 'verify against spec' instead of assuming them, and it asks the key questions about the limit rules and ToS re-acceptance. B is better structured for attaching to the ticket and meets the criteria more directly.
